profile.name: Dhathathreyan Natarajan
profile.headline: Data Science & Economics at NUS · Python, machine learning and financial modelling
profile.about:
I'm a Data Science and Economics undergraduate at the National University of Singapore. I like taking messy, real-world data and turning it into something people can make decisions with, whether that's a forecast, a valuation or a policy recommendation.

Before university I served as a Combat Engineer Officer in the Singapore Armed Forces, where I led explosives training for 100 soldiers and took my unit through two major evaluations. It taught me to plan carefully, stay calm under pressure and own the outcome.

Since then I've built a Python emissions-compliance optimiser for a shipping company's fleet, forecast humidity with LSTM and XGBoost models, built a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline for maritime regulations, and valued companies with DCF models for stock pitch competitions. I also tutor mathematics at Tim Gan Math. I'm happiest where data science meets economics and finance.

projects.title: ARROW: Maritime Intelligence Platform
projects.summary: A shipbroking platform that pairs an AI market briefing (RAG) with route optimisation and fuel-strategy analysis.
projects.description:
Shipbrokers negotiate fixtures between shipowners and charterers using a mix of regulations, market reports and route knowledge scattered across dozens of documents. For the ARROW case competition our team built a web platform that brings this together: define a cargo and route, plan the voyage, compare fuel strategies, and get an AI-written market briefing grounded in real regulatory and market documents.

My part was the RAG pipeline behind the briefings and the AI assistant, which answers questions with maritime information drawn only from the document library.
approach: Indexed a library of 15 maritime documents (SOLAS, MARPOL, the ISM and ISPS codes, BIMCO charter parties, ISO 8217 fuel standards and Veson market reports) into a Chroma vector store using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings.
Retrieved the most relevant passages for each voyage's inputs (ports, cargo, fuel type, laycan dates) and listed the source documents alongside each answer.

Prompted Mistral-7B-Instruct (via Hugging Face) to write a structured 800–900-word broker briefing covering route risks, cargo market conditions, fuel and compliance costs, negotiation leverage and valuation ranges, using only the retrieved context.
Served the pipeline as a Flask API, packaged with Docker, that feeds the platform's dashboard and chat assistant.

The team's route optimiser generated 3,789 candidate sea routes between export and import ports (direct and via hub ports), flagged high-risk war zones and ranked routes by distance, port charges and expected demurrage.

The fuel-strategy module compares a baseline fuel mix against alternative fuels and energy-saving devices over the vessel's life, with carbon pooling prices, discounting, ROI and price-sensitivity analysis.
highlights: End-to-end prototype: web dashboard, RAG briefing API and route optimiser working together
Briefings cite the regulatory and market documents they draw from, so brokers can check every claim
3,789 pre-computed routes, mapped interactively with Folium

projects.title: Capcom Equity Research: Nanyang Capital Stock Pitch
projects.summary: A BUY call on Capcom (TSE: 9697) with a ¥4,800 base-case target, built on a full three-statement and DCF model.
projects.role: Built the financial model and investment thesis
projects.description:
Capcom's share price had fallen about 27% from its peak after the troubled launch of Monster Hunter Wilds, as investors worried that FY2025 had been the top of the cycle. For the Nanyang Capital Stock Pitch 2026 I argued the market was wrong: catalog sales were accelerating, guidance pointed to a 13th straight year of record profit, and upcoming launches weren't priced in.

I built the valuation from Capcom's annual and integrated reports: segment-level revenue projections, three financial statements, a DCF, peer comparison and probability-weighted scenarios.
approach: Compiled five years of financials (FY2021–FY2025) and projected revenue by segment (Digital Contents, Arcade Operations, Amusement Equipment, Other) to FY2028, driven by unit sales of major titles and catalog growth.
Built the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow projections, then valued the company by DCF (WACC 8.7%, terminal growth 2.5%) weighted with comparable-company multiples and scenario analysis.
Benchmarked Capcom against gaming peers on EV/EBITDA, P/E, operating margin and revenue growth to test whether its valuation premium was justified.
Wrote a variant view on five market concerns and mapped catalysts (Resident Evil Requiem launch, Monster Hunter Wilds DLC, Switch 2 ports) against consensus estimates.
Set bear, base and bull cases with explicit revenue, margin, EPS and exit-multiple assumptions, plus a structured risk matrix with mitigants.
highlights: Probability-weighted target of ¥4,550 across bear (¥2,800), base (¥4,800) and bull (¥5,400) cases
Full model shared below: assumptions, statements, valuation, sensitivity and thesis tabs

projects.title: Weather Humidity Forecasting
projects.summary: Forecasting relative humidity 1, 6 and 24 hours ahead with Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM and a hybrid LSTM-XGBoost model.
projects.role: Built the forecasting models; wrote the Pandas preprocessing pipeline and the stationarity and correlation analysis
projects.description: Relative humidity matters for weather forecasting, public health and environmental monitoring, but it's hard to predict because weather variables interact in complex, non-linear ways. Using 100,057 hourly observations from 2010 to 2021, we built and compared four machine learning models to forecast humidity 1, 6 and 24 hours ahead, without using current humidity as an input.
approach: Explored the data first: correlation matrix, ACF and PACF plots, ADF and KPSS stationarity tests, and rolling statistics, which revealed strong 24-hour seasonality.
Wrote the preprocessing pipeline in Pandas: removed physically impossible readings, standardised features and built 1-, 6- and 24-hour lag windows without leaking the target.
Built a Random Forest baseline, then XGBoost with seasonal, lag, difference and interaction features, validated with time-series cross-validation.
Built LSTM models in Keras and tuned units, dropout, learning rate, batch size and epochs separately for each horizon using Bayesian optimisation (Optuna).
Built a hybrid model that feeds features learned by the LSTM into a tuned XGBoost model.
highlights: XGBoost was the best model at every horizon: MAE 0.046 (1h), 0.064 (6h) and 0.080 (24h)
Errors are comparable to the 5–10% typical of human forecasters
Showed the hybrid LSTM-XGBoost didn't beat its parts, and explained why

projects.title: HDB Resale Price Regression Model
projects.summary: A statistically rigorous linear model of Singapore HDB resale prices that explains 88.6% of price variation.
projects.description: The goal was to build the best possible linear regression model for HDB resale prices that also satisfies the standard regression assumptions, so its coefficients can be trusted and interpreted. The data covers 2,456 resale transactions from July 2020 (data.gov.sg).
approach: Explored the price distribution (right-skewed, skewness 1.04) and engineered features: remaining lease in decimal years, storey midpoints and flat age.
Detected perfect multicollinearity between remaining lease, flat age and lease start date (|r| = 0.9993) and kept only one of them.
Fitted a baseline model, then used Box-Cox analysis (optimal λ = −0.38) to compare log and reciprocal square-root transformations, choosing the log for interpretability.
Ran stepwise AIC selection, VIF checks, influence diagnostics (Cook's distance) and full residual checks for normality, constant variance, linearity and independence.
Interpreted every coefficient as a percentage price effect, e.g. +0.89% per extra square metre and a 43% premium for the Central Area.
highlights: Adjusted R² of 0.886, up from 0.841 for the untransformed baseline
All regression assumptions checked and satisfied; no highly influential points

projects.title: Predicting HDB Resale Prices with Machine Learning
projects.summary: Comparing linear regression, decision trees, k-NN and principal component regression to predict HDB resale prices.
projects.description: Buyers and sellers make better decisions when they understand what drives HDB resale prices. Working with a dataset of flat characteristics, I reduced 230 candidate predictors to 133, then built and compared four predictive models, judging them by RMSE and margin of error against the mean price of about $497,000.
approach: Log-transformed the right-skewed resale price to stabilise variance and reduce the pull of extreme values.
Used a 4,000/2,000 train-test split and 10-fold cross-validation for every model.
Built a linear model with forward selection (91 predictors), a decision tree tuned on the complexity parameter, and k-NN tuned on k.
Applied PCA to keep 95% of the variance, cutting 133 predictors to 69 components, and fitted a principal component regression.
highlights: Principal component regression was the most accurate: RMSE $40,092, an 8.06% margin of error
Beat linear regression (10.34%), decision tree (11.07%) and k-NN (15.12%)
Discussed limitations and next steps, such as ridge regression and adding economic factors like housing grants

projects.title: Raising Singapore's Female Labour Force Participation
projects.summary: NTU x MOM essay competition: a data-driven country similarity index and a policy proposal for Singapore.
projects.role: Built the machine learning similarity index; co-wrote the policy analysis
projects.description:
Singapore's female labour force participation rate (61.25% in 2024) lags global leaders like Iceland (70.3%). Policies only transfer well between similar countries, so before studying what other countries do, we used data to find the countries most like Singapore.

We then evaluated their parental leave, childcare, equal pay and four-day-week policies through three economic frameworks, and designed a proposal suited to Singapore.
approach: Combined country-level data on female participation trends, female working hours, GDP per capita, purchasing power, cost of living and a broader similarity index.
Cleaned and matched country names across sources with fuzzy matching, and imputed missing values from the nearest similar countries.
Weighted each metric by its correlation with female participation and scored every country's distance from Singapore, identifying Iceland, New Zealand and Vietnam as the closest comparators.
Evaluated their policies using Human Capital Theory, Feminist Economics and Institutional Path Dependence.
Proposed Community-Supported Workplace Childcare Co-operatives: employer-supported, government-subsidised childcare hubs with AI-driven scheduling and a 32-hour work week.
highlights: Data-driven selection of comparator countries rather than picking them by intuition
A concrete, Singapore-specific policy proposal grounded in evidence from Iceland, New Zealand, Vietnam and Quebec
